sections.overview: The blue mussel is a bivalve mollusc of cool northern coasts. It anchors itself to rocks and to other mussels with tough threads and forms dense beds that shelter many other animals and plants. It is also widely eaten and farmed.
sections.identification: The solid shell is roughly triangular and smooth, with concentric growth lines but no ribs, usually purple or blue and sometimes brown, with a pearl-white interior. Adults are typically 5 to 10 cm, though some populations stay at 2 to 3 cm and the largest reach 15 to 20 cm. It is easily confused with the Mediterranean mussel, and no single feature separates the species reliably. The consulted species references do not provide a reliable adult body mass for identification; no weight is estimated here.
sections.habitat: It lives from the high intertidal zone to shallow subtidal water, roughly 0 to 5 m deep, on open rocky coasts, in crevices, on piers and in estuaries. In the north-east Atlantic it ranges from the White Sea to southern France, and in the west Atlantic from the Canadian Maritimes to North Carolina.
sections.diet: It is a suspension feeder that filters bacteria, phytoplankton, detritus and dissolved organic matter from the water. It can feed only while submerged, so growth is slower higher on the shore.
sections.behavior: Mussels are bound together by byssus threads into beds up to five or six layers deep. A detached mussel can make new threads within 24 hours, and several mussels can work together to immobilise a predatory snail with their threads. Settlement of young mussels is gregarious, often among established adults.
sections.reproduction: Sexes are separate and fertilisation is external, with spawning from April to September, peaking in spring and summer. Females release millions of eggs, up to about 40 million in the largest, and maturity comes at 1 to 2 years. The larvae feed in the plankton for typically 1 to 6 months, and may delay settling for up to 40 days at 10 °C.
sections.ecology: Predation is the main cause of death. Dog whelks, starfish, crabs, sea urchins, flatfish and birds such as oystercatchers, eiders and gulls eat mussels, and in the Ythan estuary birds took 72% of annual mussel production. Mussel beds provide hard surface for algae and spaces for worms and other animals, and can host parasites and commensals.
sections.conservation: The species is common and abundant in many coastal areas, and the Animal Diversity Web lists no special status. Over-exploitation of small beds can reduce recruitment, and mussels can accumulate pathogens and algal toxins, which matters for people who eat them.
